lines.text: Pharmacology asks two questions: what does the drug do to the body (pharmacodynamics), and what does the body do to the drug (pharmacokinetics)?
Drug: a substance used to prevent, diagnose or treat disease.
Poison: any chemical that causes harm. Toxin: a poison of biological origin.
Pharmacokinetics = absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion (ADME).
Toxicology: harmful effects of chemicals. Many drugs become poisons at high doses.
Pharmacogenetics: why genes make people respond differently to drugs.
Pharmacovigilance: monitoring and reporting adverse drug effects.
“What the body does to the drug” = pharmacokinetics. “What the drug does to the body” = pharmacodynamics.
Every drug comes from somewhere (plant, animal, mineral, microbe, lab) and has three names. Nurses and prescriptions use the generic name.
Plants: morphine, digoxin, atropine, quinine. Animals: insulin, heparin. Minerals: magnesium sulfate, ferrous sulfate.
Microbes: penicillin, streptomycin. Synthetic: aspirin, paracetamol. Genetic engineering: human insulin.
Chemical name: describes the structure; too complex for prescriptions.
Generic name: international, given by WHO (e.g. paracetamol).
Brand name: owned by the company; one drug can have many (e.g. Panadol, Adol for paracetamol).
Prescription-only drugs: antibiotics, narcotics, psychotropics. Over-the-counter: vitamins, antacids, simple painkillers.
Paracetamol vs Panadol: paracetamol is the generic name; Panadol is a brand.
The dosage form is the physical shape a drug comes in. It decides how it is given and how fast it acts.
Liquids: solutions, suspensions, emulsions.
Semi-solids: ointments, creams, pastes, jellies.
Solids: powders, granules, tablets, capsules, suppositories.
Gases: inhalations.
A suppository is a solid dosage form.
A new drug is tested first in animals, then in humans in four phases, from a few healthy volunteers to the whole market.
Phase I: first time in humans; 20–80 healthy volunteers; finds the dose where toxicity starts.
Phase II: first time in patients; 80–100 people; checks efficacy and the best dose.
Phase III: hundreds to thousands of patients; confirms efficacy, finds less common effects.
Phase IV: after marketing; post-marketing surveillance.
Anticancer drugs are not tested in healthy volunteers in phase I.
Post-marketing surveillance = phase IV.
Oral is the most common, safest and cheapest route, but slow and affected by food and the liver. Sublingual skips the liver and works fast.
Oral advantages: safe, convenient, cheap, painless, self-given.
Oral disadvantages: slow (not for emergencies), not for unconscious or vomiting patients, destroyed by acid or enzymes, first-pass metabolism.
Sublingual: tablet under the tongue; lipid-soluble drugs absorb quickly straight into the superior vena cava, avoiding first-pass (e.g. nitroglycerin).
Sublingual is only for small doses, and some drugs taste bad.
Why is nitroglycerin given sublingually? To avoid first-pass metabolism in the liver.
Parenteral = given by injection, bypassing the gut. Faster and more exact, but needs sterile technique and is harder to undo.
Used when the drug isn't absorbed or is destroyed in the gut, irritates the gut, is needed fast, or the patient is unconscious.
IM: deep into muscle (deltoid, gluteus). IV: bolus or infusion. SC: under the skin, non-irritant drugs only.
SC absorption is slow (fewer vessels); good for self-injection and depot preparations.
Disadvantages: little time to reverse an overdose, needs sterile drugs and asepsis, painful, expensive.
IV bioavailability is 100%.
In shock, SC injections absorb poorly because skin blood flow falls.
These routes treat local problems or help when the mouth can't be used.
Rectal: unconscious or vomiting patients, children (paracetamol suppository), irritant drugs; less first-pass than oral. But absorption is slow and irregular.
Vaginal: pessaries for local conditions (e.g. miconazole); avoids first-pass.
Inhalation: very fast absorption through the alveoli (salbutamol, beclomethasone); dose is hard to control.
Topical: skin, eye, mucous membranes. Transdermal patches give slow, steady systemic effect (nicotine, nitroglycerin, scopolamine).
Eye drops are meant to act locally; little drains into the body.
Child who is vomiting and has fever → paracetamol suppository.
To reach the blood, most drugs must cross cell membranes, which are made of fat. Fat-soluble drugs cross easily; water-soluble ones need pores or carriers.
Simple diffusion: high → low concentration, no carrier, no energy. Most drugs enter this way.
Filtration: small water-soluble molecules pass through pores.
Facilitated diffusion: carrier, no energy, can be saturated.
Active transport: carrier + energy, moves against the gradient.
Endocytosis: the cell engulfs very large molecules (e.g. oral polio vaccine).
Moving against a concentration gradient needs energy → active transport.
Absorption depends on the drug (charge, solubility), the gut (pH, food, motility, blood flow) and the patient (age, disease).
Un-ionized drug is fat-soluble and absorbs well; ionized drug absorbs poorly.
Weak acids (aspirin) absorb in the stomach; weak bases (pethidine, ephedrine) in the small intestine.
Empty stomach → faster. Irritant drugs (aspirin, iron) are given after food.
Vitamin C increases iron absorption. Milk and antacids (calcium) block tetracycline.
The intestine absorbs more than the stomach because it has much more blood flow.
Heart failure (gut edema, less blood flow) and liver cirrhosis also change absorption.
Tetracycline taken with milk → less absorbed (calcium complex).
Bioavailability = how much of the dose actually reaches the blood. IV is 100%; other routes lose some on the way.
Example: 100 mg given by mouth, 70 mg reaches the blood → bioavailability 70%.
First-pass effect: the liver or gut wall breaks down part of an oral drug before it reaches the circulation.
Nitroglycerin: over 90% destroyed by first pass.
Very water-soluble or very fat-soluble drugs absorb poorly.
Some drugs are destroyed in the gut: penicillin G by acid, insulin by enzymes.
Formulation matters: particle size, salt form, enteric coating change dissolution.
Why can't insulin be taken by mouth? Gut enzymes destroy it.
Once in the blood, a drug spreads into tissues. How far it goes depends on blood flow, fat solubility, protein binding and barriers.
Well-perfused organs (lung, brain, liver, kidney) get the drug faster than muscle and fat.
Only free (unbound) drug works. Albumin carries acidic drugs; α1-acid glycoprotein carries basic drugs.
Some drugs collect in certain tissues: gentamicin in kidney, chloroquine in liver, tetracycline and lead in bone, thiopental in fat.
Blood-brain barrier: only fat-soluble or carrier-transported drugs get in.
Meningitis opens the barrier, so drugs that normally can't enter now can.
Why do some antibiotics reach the CSF only in meningitis? Inflammation makes the barrier leaky.
The kidney can't remove fat-soluble drugs, so the liver changes them into water-soluble forms that can be excreted.
Phase I: oxidation, reduction or hydrolysis adds or exposes a polar group. The drug may become more active, less active, or unchanged.
Cytochrome P450 (CYP450) is the main phase I enzyme system.
Phase II (conjugation): the drug is joined to a body substance (glucuronide, sulfate, acetyl, glycine, methyl).
Genes: slow vs fast acetylators (INH, hydralazine, dapsone).
Age: newborns can't handle chloramphenicol (gray baby syndrome); the elderly metabolize more slowly.
Liver disease and heart failure slow metabolism.
Gray baby syndrome → chloramphenicol in a newborn.
Some drugs speed up the liver enzymes (inducers) and others slow them down (inhibitors). That is the cause of many dangerous drug interactions.
Inducers make other drugs disappear faster → less effect.
Classic example: rifampicin or phenobarbitone + oral contraceptive pill → pill fails → unwanted pregnancy.
Inhibitors slow breakdown of other drugs → higher levels and toxicity.
Classic example: cimetidine + warfarin → warfarin builds up → bleeding risk.
Patient on the pill starts rifampicin → contraceptive failure (enzyme induction).
The kidney removes most drugs. The liver (bile), lungs and minor routes (sweat, saliva, milk) remove the rest.
Glomerular filtration: only free (unbound) drug is filtered.
Tubular secretion: active carriers in the proximal tubule push drugs into urine.
Tubular reabsorption: uncharged drug can go back into the blood.
Alkalinizing urine helps remove weak acids; acidifying urine helps remove weak bases.
Biliary excretion + reabsorption from the gut (enterohepatic circulation) prolongs action (e.g. oral estrogen, chloramphenicol).
Total clearance = hepatic + renal + pulmonary + other; liver and kidney matter most.
Aspirin (weak acid) overdose → alkalinize the urine to remove it faster.
Half-life is the time for the drug level to fall by half. It tells you how often to dose and how long a drug stays.
Half-life gets longer with less kidney or liver blood flow and slower metabolism.
First-order: a constant FRACTION is removed per unit time. Most drugs.
Zero-order: a constant AMOUNT is removed per unit time, so the drug can build up to toxic levels. Examples: ethanol, phenytoin.
Half-life decides the dosing interval and how long to reach steady state.
Which drugs follow zero-order kinetics? Ethanol and phenytoin.

notes.title: Therapeutic range, steady state & loading dose

lines.text: The goal of dosing is to keep the drug level inside the therapeutic window: above the minimum effective level, below the toxic level.
Repeated doses reach a plateau (steady state) when elimination equals the dose given.
Loading dose: a large first dose to reach the plateau quickly.
Maintenance dose: equals what is eliminated each day, to keep the level steady.
Continuous infusion or smaller, more frequent doses reduce peaks and troughs.
A big first dose to reach the target level fast = loading dose.
Most drugs work by binding to a receptor, like a key in a lock. A few work by simple chemistry (antacids, charcoal).
Receptor: a protein that a drug or body chemical binds to, producing an effect.
Four families: ion channels, G-protein-coupled receptors, enzyme-linked receptors, intracellular receptors.
G-protein receptors work through second messengers: cAMP, calcium, cGMP, IP3.
Covalent bonds are the strongest; covalent drug–receptor binding is usually irreversible.
Antacids don't use receptors; they neutralize acid chemically.
Potency = how little drug you need. Efficacy = how big the maximum effect can be. Efficacy matters more for treatment.
Potency is measured by EC50, the dose giving 50% of the maximum effect.
Affinity = ability to bind the receptor.
Full agonist: binds and gives the maximum response (adrenaline, morphine).
Partial agonist: binds but gives less than maximum (pentazocine).
Inverse agonist: produces the opposite effect to the agonist.
A drug with greater efficacy is more useful than one that is merely more potent.
An antagonist does nothing on its own; it blocks or opposes another drug or body chemical.
Chemical: the antidote reacts directly with the drug, e.g. dimercaprol binds mercury, arsenic, gold.
Functional (physiological): acts on a different receptor with the opposite effect, e.g. adrenaline vs histamine bronchoconstriction.
Competitive: competes for the same receptor; the most common type. E.g. propranolol, atropine, naloxone.
Competitive can be reversible (loose bond) or irreversible (covalent bond).
Competitive antagonists have affinity but no intrinsic activity.
Adrenaline reversing histamine's bronchospasm in anaphylaxis → functional (physiological) antagonism.
The therapeutic index tells you how safe a drug is: the bigger the gap between the effective and toxic dose, the safer.
Graded response: the effect grows smoothly with the dose.
Quantal response: all-or-none, measured as how many people respond.
ED50: dose effective in 50% of people. LD50 (or TD50): dose lethal (or toxic) in 50%.
Therapeutic index = LD50 / ED50 (or TD50 / ED50). Higher = safer.
Warfarin has a narrow index (risky); penicillin has a wide one (safe).
Narrow therapeutic index drugs (digoxin, warfarin) need blood level monitoring.
With repeated use, the body can respond less (tolerance) or more (sensitization) to the same dose.
Tolerance: more drug needed for the same effect; curve shifts right. Can cross to similar drugs.
Sensitization: less drug needed; curve shifts left (e.g. amphetamine).
Causes: less drug reaching the site, receptor down-regulation, faster metabolism, learned responses.
Same dose works less over time → tolerance.
One drug can change another's level (pharmacokinetic) or its effect (pharmacodynamic). Interactions can help or harm.
Additive: effect = the sum of both (1 + 1 = 2).
Synergistic: effect greater than the sum (1 + 1 = 3), e.g. alcohol with sedatives.
Antagonistic: effect less than the sum.
Cumulative: repeated doses build up a bigger effect than the first.
Alcohol + benzodiazepine → synergistic CNS depression.
Type A reactions are predictable from what the drug does and are common. Type B are unpredictable (allergy, genetics) and more dangerous.
A (augmented): dose-related, 75% of ADRs. E.g. bleeding with warfarin, hypoglycemia with insulin.
B (bizarre): not dose-related; allergy or idiosyncrasy. Stop the drug.
C (chronic): long-term use, e.g. NSAID kidney damage.
D (delayed): e.g. thalidomide birth defects, cancer.
E (end of use): withdrawal or rebound, e.g. stopping β-blockers → rebound tachycardia and hypertension.
F: failure of efficacy.
Higher ADR risk: polypharmacy, elderly, children, pregnancy, multiple diseases, malnutrition.
Hypoglycemia from too much insulin → type A (augmented).
These four words are easy to confuse, and exams love them.
Side effect: unwanted but expected at normal dose, e.g. sedation with antihistamines. Can be useful elsewhere (codeine constipation for diarrhea).
Secondary effect: an indirect result, e.g. steroids weaken immunity and latent TB activates.
Toxic effect: from overdose or long use, e.g. AV block from digoxin, bleeding from heparin.
Intolerance: toxic effects at a normal dose in a sensitive person, e.g. ataxia after a few doses of carbamazepine.
Idiosyncrasy: a genetic, abnormal reaction, e.g. aplastic anemia with chloramphenicol, excitement with barbiturates.
Genetically determined abnormal reaction → idiosyncrasy.
Drug allergy is an immune reaction, not related to how the drug normally works. It can happen even with a tiny dose.
Type I: anaphylactic. Type II: cytolytic. Type III: Arthus (immune complex). Type IV: delayed, cell-mediated.
Phototoxic: drug in the skin absorbs UVB → sunburn-like damage.
Photoallergic: immune reaction triggered by UVA → eczema-like rash. Drugs: sulfonamides, chloroquine, chlorpromazine, griseofulvin.
Anaphylaxis to penicillin → type I hypersensitivity.
Physical dependence means the body needs the drug to function normally; stopping it causes withdrawal.
Drugs causing physical dependence: opioids, barbiturates, alcohol, benzodiazepines.
Psychological dependence (habituation): mild discomfort on stopping, e.g. tea, coffee, tobacco.
Addiction: compulsive use that takes over other activities.
Withdrawal reactions: suddenly stopping steroids → acute adrenal insufficiency.
Long-term steroids stopped suddenly → adrenal crisis. Always taper.
Some drugs damage the unborn baby. The most dangerous time is organ formation, days 18–55 of pregnancy.
Days 0–17: pregnancy may fail, often unnoticed.
Days 18–55: organogenesis, the most vulnerable; malformations happen here.
Day 56 on: growth and function problems.
Examples: ACE inhibitors, thalidomide, warfarin, barbiturates.
Iatrogenic disease examples: hepatitis from INH and rifampin, peptic ulcer from aspirin and steroids, retinal damage from chloroquine.
Most vulnerable period for drug-induced malformations → 18–55 days (organogenesis).
Pharmacovigilance is detecting, reporting and preventing drug harms after drugs reach patients. Nurses play a role by reporting ADRs.
Activities: post-marketing surveillance, voluntary ADR reporting, prescription event monitoring.
Results: drug alerts, label changes, warnings, or withdrawal of a drug.
ADR severity: minor, moderate, severe (life-threatening), lethal.
ADR that is life-threatening or causes permanent damage → severe.

The autonomic nervous system runs the body automatically. Sympathetic = “fight or flight” (noradrenaline). Parasympathetic = “rest and digest” (acetylcholine). Most ANS drugs either copy or block one of these two.
Sympathetic nerves leave the thoracic and lumbar spine; the main transmitter is noradrenaline; receptors are α1, α2, β1, β2, β3.
Parasympathetic nerves leave the brain and sacral spine; the transmitter is acetylcholine; receptors are nicotinic (NN, NM) and muscarinic (M1–M5).
Four drug groups: cholinergic agonists, cholinergic blockers, adrenergic agonists, adrenergic blockers.
Parasympathetic transmitter → acetylcholine. Sympathetic → mainly noradrenaline.

notes.title: What each receptor does in the body

lines.text: If you know what each receptor does, you can predict what almost every ANS drug will do, and its side effects.
Heart: β1 → faster and stronger. M2 → slower and weaker.
Lungs: β2 → bronchodilation. M3 → bronchoconstriction.
Skin and gut vessels: α1 → constriction. Muscle vessels: β2 → dilation.
Gut: sympathetic slows it; M3 speeds it up and increases secretions.
Eye: α1 → pupil dilates (mydriasis). M3 → pupil constricts (miosis) and focuses near.
Bladder: β2 relaxes it and α1 closes the sphincter → urine is held. M3 → voiding.
Kidney: β1 → renin release. Uterus: β2 relaxes; M3 contracts.
A drug that blocks M3 → dry mouth, dilated pupils, urine retention, constipation. That is the atropine pattern.
Bethanechol is a muscarinic stimulant that “wakes up” a lazy bladder or gut after surgery or delivery.
It acts on muscarinic receptors (not nicotinic), mainly in the bladder and GI tract, and is not broken down by AChE.
Uses: non-obstructive urinary retention after surgery or childbirth; post-operative intestinal atony.
Acetylcholine itself is not used as a drug: it acts everywhere and is destroyed too quickly by AChE.
Urinary retention after delivery, no obstruction → bethanechol.
Glaucoma = fluid builds up in the eye and pressure damages the optic nerve. Pilocarpine opens the drainage so fluid can flow out.
It contracts the ciliary muscle and the iris sphincter (M3), which opens the trabecular meshwork.
Aqueous humor drains into the canal of Schlemm, and eye pressure falls.
Drug of choice for emergency lowering of eye pressure in both open-angle and angle-closure glaucoma.
Also reverses pupil dilation caused by muscarinic blockers.
Open-angle glaucoma first line: prostaglandin analogues, β-blockers (timolol), carbonic anhydrase inhibitors.
Angle-closure glaucoma is an emergency: pilocarpine + osmotic agent + a drug that reduces fluid production. Surgery (iridectomy) is the definitive fix.
Acute angle-closure glaucoma → pilocarpine is part of emergency treatment, but iridectomy is the cure.
These drugs block the enzyme that destroys acetylcholine, so acetylcholine lasts longer. Key use: myasthenia gravis.
Edrophonium: very short (10–20 min); used to diagnose myasthenia gravis.
Physostigmine: enters the brain; used for atropine (anticholinergic) overdose, and gut or bladder atony.
Neostigmine: doesn't enter the brain; stimulates bladder and gut, reverses non-depolarizing muscle relaxants, treats myasthenia gravis.
Pyridostigmine: longer acting (3–6 h); chronic treatment of myasthenia gravis.
Donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine: slow Alzheimer's disease (they can't stop it). Main side effect: GI upset.
Too much: convulsions (physostigmine), slow heart, and muscle paralysis.
Atropine overdose → physostigmine, because it reaches the brain.
Organophosphate insecticides lock up acetylcholinesterase permanently. Acetylcholine floods every synapse, causing a cholinergic crisis.
They bind AChE covalently (irreversibly).
Acetylcholine builds up for a long time at all sites where it is released.
Examples: malathion, parathion, diazinon (insecticides); sarin, soman, tabun (nerve gases).
Treatment step 1: decontaminate and reduce absorption.
Step 2: atropine, the cornerstone of treatment.
Step 3: pralidoxime (2-PAM), but only before the enzyme “ages”.
Farmer after spraying insecticide, with salivation, sweating and pinpoint pupils → atropine first.

flags.text: Her ANS file does not list the symptoms of organophosphate poisoning. The usual teaching is SLUDGE (salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, GI upset, emesis) + small pupils + bradycardia. Check her First Aid notes.

lines.text: Atropine blocks muscarinic receptors, the opposite of the parasympathetic system. It dries, dilates and speeds up.
Blocks M receptors only, not nicotinic.
Eye: dilated pupil, can't focus near. Gut: strong antispasmodic. Glands: dry mouth.
Heart: low doses slightly slow it; higher doses speed it up.
Uses: eye exams, gut spasm, bradycardia, drying secretions before surgery, antidote for cholinergic poisoning.
Side effects: dry mouth, blurred vision, fast heart rate, urine retention, constipation.
Toxic doses: restlessness, confusion, hallucinations, delirium, then collapse.
Antidote for atropine overdose: physostigmine.
Organophosphate poisoning, or bradycardia from digoxin toxicity → atropine.
Atropine's relatives each have one special job: motion sickness, COPD, eye exams, Parkinsonism, or overactive bladder.
Scopolamine: best drug for motion sickness; also post-op nausea. Causes sedation and memory loss; can be abused.
Ipratropium, tiotropium (inhaled): bronchodilators for COPD; ipratropium also in acute asthma.
Benztropine, trihexyphenidyl: Parkinsonism, including EPS caused by antipsychotics.
Tropicamide (6 h) and cyclopentolate (24 h): eye drops for dilation; shorter than atropine.
Oxybutynin, tolterodine, solifenacin: overactive bladder.
A patient on haloperidol develops tremor and stiffness → benztropine.
Used in surgery to fully relax skeletal muscle. They block acetylcholine at the muscle, and neostigmine can reverse them.
They compete with acetylcholine at nicotinic receptors on muscle, so the muscle can't depolarize → flaccid paralysis for 30–60 min.
Drugs: vecuronium, rocuronium, pancuronium, atracurium, cisatracurium.
Given IV only; they aren't absorbed by mouth.
Reversed by AChE inhibitors: neostigmine, edrophonium.
Made stronger by: inhaled anesthetics, aminoglycosides, calcium channel blockers.
Reversing rocuronium at the end of surgery → neostigmine.
The only depolarizing muscle relaxant. Very fast onset, which makes it the choice for rapid intubation.
It depolarizes the muscle like acetylcholine but isn't broken down by AChE, so the muscle stays paralyzed.
It is broken down by plasma pseudocholinesterase.
Uses: rapid endotracheal intubation (reduces aspiration risk); electroconvulsive therapy.
Malignant hyperthermia when combined with inhaled anesthetics → treat with dantrolene.
Prolonged apnea in people with pseudocholinesterase deficiency.
Hyperkalemia.
High fever and rigidity during surgery with halothane + succinylcholine → malignant hyperthermia → dantrolene.
Sympathomimetics copy the sympathetic system. Which receptor a drug hits decides what it does.
Catecholamines (adrenaline, noradrenaline, dopamine, dobutamine): very potent, short-acting, destroyed by MAO and COMT, don't enter the brain.
Non-catecholamines (ephedrine, phenylephrine, amphetamine): longer acting, some enter the brain.
Direct acting = act on receptors. Indirect = release noradrenaline or block its reuptake (amphetamine, cocaine). Mixed = both (ephedrine).
Adrenaline: α1, α2, β1, β2. Noradrenaline: α1, α2, β1.
Dobutamine: β1. Phenylephrine: α1. Salbutamol, terbutaline: β2.
Catecholamines can't be taken by mouth: gut and liver enzymes destroy them.
Adrenaline stimulates every α and β receptor. That makes it the life-saving drug in anaphylaxis and cardiac arrest.
Heart (β1): faster, stronger, faster conduction.
Vessels: α1 constricts skin and gut vessels; β2 dilates muscle vessels. Low dose → β effects; high dose → α effects.
Lungs (β2): strong bronchodilator; also stops mast cells releasing histamine.
Metabolism: raises blood sugar and breaks down fat.
Uses: anaphylactic shock, cardiac arrest, acute asthma, prolonging local anesthetics, stopping local bleeding.
Side effects: arrhythmias, angina, cerebral hemorrhage, anxiety, tremor, pulmonary edema.
Contraindicated: severe hypertension, fast arrhythmias, coronary artery disease.
Given IV, IM or SC. Doesn't work by mouth.
Diabetics may need more insulin; non-selective β-blockers leave its α effect unopposed → BP rises sharply.
Why is adrenaline added to lidocaine? It constricts vessels, so the anesthetic stays longer.
α1-agonists squeeze blood vessels. Used to raise low BP and to clear a blocked nose.
Phenylephrine: treats hypotension in hospitalized or surgical patients; nasal decongestant; eye drops to dilate the pupil.
Phenylephrine raises BP, which causes a reflex slow heart rate.
Oxymetazoline: nasal spray and eye-redness drops. Long use → rebound congestion and dependence.
Methyldopa (an α2-agonist): mainly for hypertension in pregnancy; side effects sedation, dry mouth, impotence.
Using a decongestant nasal spray for weeks → rebound congestion.
Dopamine does different things at different doses: low dose helps the kidneys, medium dose helps the heart, high dose squeezes vessels.
Low dose (2–5 μg/kg/min): D1 receptors dilate kidney vessels, more urine. Used in shock.
Moderate dose (5–10 μg/kg/min): β1, stronger heartbeat. Acute heart failure and shock.
High dose (10–30 μg/kg/min): α1, vasoconstriction and reduced kidney blood flow.
Dobutamine: β1 only; preferred for acute decompensated heart failure.
Dopamine: IV only, half-life 3–5 minutes.
Low-dose dopamine → kidney (D1). High dose → vasoconstriction (α1).
β2 agonists open the airways. Salbutamol is the rescue inhaler for an asthma attack.
Short acting (salbutamol, terbutaline): inhaled for acute bronchospasm; works in 1–5 min, lasts 2–6 h.
Long acting: salmeterol, formoterol.
Ephedrine: mixed acting, works by mouth, enters the brain; for asthma, nasal congestion, raising BP. Now used less.
Acute asthma attack → inhaled short-acting β2 agonist (salbutamol).
α1-blockers relax vessels and the prostate. Main uses: hypertension and enlarged prostate (BPH).
Prazosin, terazosin, doxazosin: lower BP and relieve BPH.
Tamsulosin: selective α1A, works on the prostate with fewer BP effects, so it is preferred for BPH.
Phentolamine: reverses tissue damage when noradrenaline leaks out of a vein; controls BP in pheochromocytoma.
Side effects: dizziness on standing, reflex fast heart rate, headache, edema.
Noradrenaline infusion leaks into the tissue → phentolamine to prevent necrosis.
β-blockers slow and calm the heart. Cardioselective ones (atenolol, metoprolol) act mainly on the heart; non-selective ones (propranolol) also narrow the airways.
β1 block: slower heart rate, slower AV conduction, weaker contraction, less oxygen demand.
β2 block (non-selective drugs): bronchoconstriction and vasoconstriction.
Uses: angina, arrhythmias, hypertension, chronic heart failure (carvedilol, metoprolol, bisoprolol), migraine and anxiety (propranolol), hyperthyroidism, portal hypertension, glaucoma (timolol).
Side effects: slow heart rate, low BP, AV block, bronchospasm, hidden hypoglycemia, cold hands, fatigue, nightmares.
Contraindicated: asthma/COPD (non-selective), bradycardia, hypotension, acute decompensated heart failure.
Esmolol has the shortest half-life (10 min).
Carvedilol and labetalol block both α1 and β.
Asthmatic patient needs a β-blocker → choose a cardioselective one; never propranolol.
Brain drugs work by boosting or blocking chemical messengers. Knowing what each messenger does explains both the drug's effect and its side effects.
GABA: main inhibitory (calming) messenger. Too little → seizures. Benzodiazepines and barbiturates boost it.
Glutamate: main excitatory messenger (NMDA receptors). Too much → seizures. Ketamine blocks NMDA.
Noradrenaline: mood, wakefulness, alertness. Too little → depression.
Dopamine: movement, behavior, prolactin; vomiting center. Too much → schizophrenia; too little → Parkinson's.
Serotonin (5-HT): mood, appetite, temperature, vomiting.
Acetylcholine: arousal, movement, learning and memory. Problems → dementia and parkinsonism.
Low dopamine in the basal ganglia → Parkinson's. Excess dopamine activity → schizophrenia.
Benzodiazepines calm the brain by boosting GABA. Low doses relieve anxiety; higher doses bring sleep. Safer than barbiturates, but addictive.
They bind the benzodiazepine site on the GABA-A receptor → more chloride enters the neuron → less firing.
They can't work without GABA, which makes them safer than barbiturates.
Uses: severe anxiety (short term only), insomnia, amnesia before procedures (midazolam), alcohol withdrawal (chlordiazepoxide, diazepam), status epilepticus (lorazepam, diazepam), muscle spasm.
Side effects: drowsiness, hangover, amnesia, ataxia, rebound insomnia.
Dependence with high dose or long use. Sudden stopping → withdrawal like alcohol (seizures, delirium). Short-acting ones (triazolam) give worse withdrawal.
Long acting: diazepam, chlordiazepoxide. Short: triazolam, midazolam.
Avoid in pregnancy (they depress the newborn), with alcohol, in acute narrow-angle glaucoma, shock, coma.
Use hypnotics only for 2–4 weeks.
Benzodiazepine + alcohol → dangerous, possibly fatal CNS depression.
Flumazenil is the antidote that reverses benzodiazepines.
Blocks the benzodiazepine site on the GABA receptor; given IV.
Fast onset, but short (half-life about 1 hour), so repeat doses may be needed for long-acting benzodiazepines.
Side effects: dizziness, nausea, vomiting, agitation. Can trigger seizures.
Benzodiazepine overdose → flumazenil. Opioid overdose → naloxone.
The old sleeping pills. Replaced by benzodiazepines because they are more dangerous: tolerance, dependence, severe withdrawal, and no antidote.
They keep the GABA chloride channel open longer; at high doses they also act without GABA.
Increasing dose: sedation → sleep → anesthesia → coma → death.
Uses today: thiopental for anesthesia; phenobarbital for epilepsy.
Side effects: drowsiness, respiratory depression, hypotension.
Strong enzyme inducers: reduce the effect of warfarin, contraceptives, steroids, β-blockers.
Overdose: no antidote. Support breathing, wash out the stomach, alkalinize urine, hemodialysis.
Why were barbiturates replaced? Low therapeutic index, dependence, enzyme induction, no antidote.
An anxiety drug that doesn't sedate and isn't addictive, but takes weeks to work.
Partial agonist at serotonin 5-HT1A receptors; does not act on GABA.
Use: generalized anxiety.
Not for panic attacks or quick relief, because the full effect takes several weeks.
No interaction with alcohol, low abuse risk, no withdrawal.
Side effects: dizziness, headache, palpitations.
Doesn't treat benzodiazepine withdrawal. With MAOIs → hypertension.
Anxious patient who needs fast relief → not buspirone.
For simple insomnia, newer drugs like zolpidem are often preferred because they disturb natural sleep less.
Zolpidem, zaleplon: act at the benzodiazepine receptor; little tolerance or rebound; side effects nightmares, amnesia, daytime drowsiness.
Ramelteon: melatonin agonist for trouble falling asleep; no abuse or dependence.
Chloral hydrate: works in 30 minutes; irritates the stomach.
Antihistamines (diphenhydramine, hydroxyzine): mild insomnia; hydroxyzine for anxiety.
β-blockers: performance anxiety (stage fright), tremor and palpitations.
SSRIs: safer than TCAs for long-term anxiety disorders.
Stage fright with tremor and palpitations → β-blocker (propranolol).
Alcohol is a CNS depressant like the sedatives, and it multiplies their effect. Benzodiazepines treat its withdrawal.
Liver: alcohol → acetaldehyde (alcohol dehydrogenase) → acetic acid (aldehyde dehydrogenase).
Synergy with benzodiazepines, antihistamines, barbiturates.
Chronic use: liver disease, gastritis, malnutrition, cardiomyopathy.
Withdrawal: benzodiazepines are the treatment of choice; carbamazepine for withdrawal seizures.
Alcohol withdrawal → benzodiazepine (diazepam or chlordiazepoxide).
Drugs that help alcoholics stop drinking: disulfiram makes drinking unpleasant; naltrexone reduces craving.
Disulfiram blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase → acetaldehyde builds up → flushing, fast heart rate, nausea when drinking.
Severe reactions: MI, heart failure, respiratory depression, death.
Metronidazole and some cephalosporins cause a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol.
Naltrexone: opioid antagonist; reduces the pleasure of drinking and craving. Better tolerated than disulfiram.
Patient on metronidazole drinks alcohol → disulfiram-like reaction.
Methanol is turned into toxic formic acid, which damages the eyes and causes acidosis.
Methanol → formaldehyde → formic acid.
Effects: respiratory failure, eye damage, metabolic acidosis.
Treatment: fomepizole, which blocks alcohol dehydrogenase.
Blurred vision and acidosis after drinking homemade alcohol → methanol → fomepizole.
A seizure is abnormal electrical activity in the brain; epilepsy is recurrent seizures. The seizure type decides the drug.
Simple partial: consciousness kept; jerking of one limb.
Complex partial: starts focal, consciousness lost.
Tonic-clonic (grand mal): stiffening then jerking. Drugs: valproate, phenytoin, carbamazepine.
Absence (petit mal): children, brief staring spells. Drugs: ethosuximide, valproate.
Myoclonic: sudden jerks. Drugs: valproate, clonazepam.
Always taper antiepileptics; stopping suddenly can cause status epilepticus.
Drugs that can cause seizures: withdrawal from alcohol or benzodiazepines, flumazenil, bupropion, clozapine, lithium.
Child with brief staring spells → absence seizure → ethosuximide or valproate. Not carbamazepine.
Status epilepticus is continuous seizures without recovery. It is an emergency: a fast benzodiazepine first, then a longer-acting drug.
Status epilepticus: IV lorazepam or diazepam, then phenytoin (or fosphenytoin). Give slowly to avoid apnea.
Febrile seizures (3 months–5 years): phenobarbital or diazepam. Phenytoin and carbamazepine don't work.
Pregnancy: one drug, lowest dose. Phenobarbital is considered safest.
Warn women of childbearing age about birth defects.
First drug for status epilepticus → IV lorazepam or diazepam.
One of the cheapest, least toxic antiepileptics, with a very long half-life.
Boosts GABA chloride flow; at high levels blocks sodium channels.
Broad use: tonic-clonic and partial seizures.
Side effects: drowsiness, lower IQ in children with long use.
Strong enzyme inducer, so many interactions.
Half-life over 50 hours; IV or oral.
Febrile seizures and seizures in pregnancy → phenobarbital is the usual drug.
A major antiepileptic that blocks sodium channels. Works for all seizures except absence, but has many side effects and interactions.
Side effects: nystagmus, ataxia, gum overgrowth (gingival hyperplasia), bone marrow suppression, liver damage.
Also: megaloblastic anemia (folate), osteomalacia (vitamin D), cleft lip and palate in the baby.
IV: can cause severe hypotension and arrhythmias.
Follows zero-order kinetics at higher doses (levels can jump).
Raised by isoniazid, cimetidine, chloramphenicol, valproate. Lowered by rifampin and barbiturates.
Contraindicated: AV block, pregnancy.
Swollen, overgrown gums in an epileptic patient → phenytoin.
Very effective for partial and tonic-clonic seizures, and the drug of choice for trigeminal neuralgia.
Uses: complex partial seizures (most effective), tonic-clonic, bipolar disorder, trigeminal neuralgia.
Can worsen absence seizures.
Side effects: drowsiness, aplastic anemia/agranulocytosis (monitor blood counts), rashes, low sodium in the elderly.
Teratogenic; contraindicated in pregnancy and bone marrow depression.
Induces its own metabolism and that of oral contraceptives.
Erythromycin, isoniazid and fluoxetine block its metabolism → toxicity after a few days.
Never with MAOIs.
Sharp facial pain on chewing (trigeminal neuralgia) → carbamazepine.
The broad-spectrum antiepileptic: works for all seizure types and is the drug of choice for absence and myoclonic seizures.
Also: mania and bipolar disorder, migraine prevention.
Side effects: nausea, hair loss, low platelets, bleeding, high ammonia.
Rare fatal liver toxicity, mainly in children under 3.
Teratogenic; contraindicated in pregnancy. Polycystic ovaries in young girls.
Inhibits liver enzymes: raises phenobarbital levels and causes phenytoin toxicity.
Not with clonazepam: can trigger absence status.
Child under 3 on valproate → watch for liver failure.
A narrow drug: it treats only absence seizures.
Blocks T-type calcium channels in the thalamus.
Mostly safe: headache, nausea, dizziness, rash; rarely blood problems or lupus-like syndrome.
Drug used ONLY for absence seizures → ethosuximide.
Newer antiepileptics have fewer interactions and less effect on thinking, but cost more.
Lamotrigine: broad use; risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome (rash).
Gabapentin: add-on for partial seizures; excreted unchanged.
Topiramate: also prevents migraine; kidney stones, weight loss, cognitive slowing.
Levetiracetam: few interactions; mood changes.
Oxcarbazepine: partial seizures; low sodium.
Felbamate: only for refractory epilepsy (aplastic anemia, liver failure).
New rash on lamotrigine → think Stevens-Johnson syndrome.
Parkinson's = not enough dopamine in the brain's movement center. Levodopa enters the brain and becomes dopamine; carbidopa stops it being wasted outside the brain.
Signs of Parkinson's: tremor, rigidity, slow movement, abnormal posture and gait.
Carbidopa blocks dopa decarboxylase outside the brain → 4–5 times less levodopa needed, fewer side effects.
Side effects: nausea and vomiting, low BP, arrhythmias, hallucinations, involuntary movements (dyskinesia), dark urine and saliva.
Works well for the first few years, then the response declines.
Pyridoxine (B6) reduces levodopa's effect.
MAOIs + levodopa → hypertensive crisis.
Antipsychotics and metoclopramide block dopamine and cancel levodopa.
Why give carbidopa with levodopa? So more levodopa reaches the brain, at a lower dose.
These make levodopa's dopamine last longer by blocking the enzymes that break it down.
Selegiline: blocks MAO-B, so more dopamine stays in the brain; reduces the levodopa dose.
Selegiline becomes amphetamine-like metabolites: give it before mid-afternoon to avoid insomnia.
High doses of selegiline also block MAO-A → risk of severe hypertension.
Entacapone, tolcapone (COMT inhibitors): more levodopa reaches the brain. Tolcapone can cause fatal liver necrosis.
Insomnia on selegiline → give it earlier in the day.
Other Parkinson's drugs either act like dopamine, release more of it, or calm the overactive acetylcholine side.
Bromocriptine, ropinirole, pramipexole: act directly on dopamine receptors; useful when levodopa response fluctuates.
Bromocriptine side effects: confusion, nausea, low BP on standing.
Amantadine: an antiviral that also releases dopamine; less effective than levodopa.
Benztropine, trihexyphenidyl: anticholinergics; only add-on drugs; dry mouth and vision problems.
Amantadine has two uses: influenza and Parkinson's.
Alzheimer's destroys acetylcholine neurons. Drugs can slow the decline a little but cannot stop the disease.
Donepezil, galantamine, rivastigmine: AChE inhibitors for mild to moderate disease.
Rivastigmine: also for dementia in Parkinson's; available as a patch.
Side effects: nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, slow heart rate, muscle cramps.
Memantine: blocks NMDA receptors; for moderate to severe disease, often with an AChE inhibitor.
Treatment of Alzheimer's is only palliative; no drug changes the disease process.
MS is an autoimmune disease that strips the myelin from nerves. Drugs calm the immune attack and relieve symptoms.
Acute attacks: corticosteroids.
Interferon: reduces relapses; side effects flu-like symptoms, depression, injection-site reactions.
Dalfampridine: improves walking speed.
Flu-like symptoms after starting interferon → expected side effect.
Schizophrenia is linked to too much dopamine activity. Typical antipsychotics block dopamine D2 receptors, which controls hallucinations and delusions, but causes movement side effects.
Drugs: chlorpromazine (the first), haloperidol, thioridazine, flupenthixol.
Work well on positive symptoms (hallucinations, delusions), poorly on negative ones (withdrawal, flat emotion).
Haloperidol: preferred for acute schizophrenia; few autonomic effects.
Side effects: EPS, low BP, high prolactin (galactorrhea, gynecomastia).
Other uses: severe nausea and vomiting (prochlorperazine), intractable hiccups (chlorpromazine).
Effect takes days to weeks.
Long-term treatment is usually needed; most patients relapse without it.
Milk from the breasts in a woman on haloperidol → high prolactin from D2 blockade.
Atypical antipsychotics block serotonin 5-HT2A more than dopamine. Fewer movement side effects, but more weight gain and diabetes.
Better for negative symptoms and resistant schizophrenia.
Clozapine: risk of agranulocytosis, so only for resistant cases; contraindicated in seizure disorders.
Olanzapine: positive and negative symptoms; also used in mania.
Side effects: weight gain, diabetes, high cholesterol.
Patient on clozapine with fever and sore throat → check WBC (agranulocytosis).
Blocking dopamine in the movement pathway (nigrostriatal) causes Parkinson-like and other movement problems.
Dystonia: sustained muscle spasms and twisting postures.
Akathisia: inner restlessness, can't sit still.
Tardive dyskinesia: late, involuntary movements of lips, tongue, neck, limbs.
Treatment of drug-induced parkinsonism: benztropine or trihexyphenidyl.
Atypical antipsychotics cause fewer EPS.
Lip smacking and tongue movements after years on chlorpromazine → tardive dyskinesia.
SSRIs boost serotonin and are the drugs of choice for depression, because they are safer and have fewer side effects than older antidepressants.
Drugs: fluoxetine, sertraline, paroxetine, citalopram, fluvoxamine.
Uses: depression, anxiety, panic, PTSD, OCD (fluvoxamine), bulimia (fluoxetine).
Side effects: anxiety, insomnia, weight change, sexual dysfunction.
Venlafaxine, duloxetine (SNRIs): when SSRIs don't work; withdrawal if stopped suddenly.
All antidepressants need at least 2 weeks to start working.
Fluoxetine has a very long half-life (~10 days for its metabolite).
Never combine with MAOIs.
Depressed patient feels no better after 5 days → normal; antidepressants need 2+ weeks.
The older antidepressants. They work, but block many other receptors, causing many side effects, and are dangerous in overdose.
Block reuptake of noradrenaline and serotonin.
Uses: depression, bedwetting in children (imipramine), neuropathic pain and migraine (amitriptyline), insomnia (doxepin).
Anticholinergic side effects: dry mouth, blurred vision, urine retention, constipation, glaucoma worsening.
Also: low BP on standing, sedation, weight gain.
Narrow therapeutic index; overdose causes arrhythmias.
With MAOIs → high fever, excitation, seizures.
TCA overdose is dangerous mainly because of heart arrhythmias.
MAOIs stop the breakdown of noradrenaline, serotonin and dopamine. Rarely used now because of dangerous food reactions.
Drugs: phenelzine, tranylcypromine.
Tyramine-rich foods (aged cheese, red wine) → hypertensive crisis.
Wait at least 2 weeks after stopping an MAOI before starting another antidepressant.
Side effects: drowsiness, low BP on standing, dry mouth, weight gain.
Patient on phenelzine eats aged cheese → hypertensive crisis.
Lithium prevents the mood swings of bipolar disorder and treats mania. It has a narrow safety margin.
Uses: acute mania and preventing bipolar relapses. Slow onset (~2 weeks).
Side effects: thirst, frequent urination, fine hand tremor, GI upset (give with food), low thyroid function.
Alternatives for bipolar: valproate, carbamazepine, lamotrigine, antipsychotics.
Thiazide and loop diuretics and NSAIDs raise lithium levels → toxicity.
Patient on lithium starts hydrochlorothiazide → risk of lithium toxicity.
Aspirin relieves pain, lowers fever, reduces inflammation, and prevents clots, all by blocking prostaglandin production.
Irreversibly blocks cyclooxygenase (COX).
Uses: mild to moderate pain, fever, arthritis, rheumatic fever; prevention of MI and TIA.
Side effects: stomach upset, GI bleeding, allergy (bronchospasm, angioedema).
Salicylism (toxicity): tinnitus, dizziness, fever, headache, hyperventilation.
Never in children or teens with flu or chickenpox → Reye's syndrome.
Avoid in the third trimester, breastfeeding and bleeding disorders.
Maximum dose 8 g/day.
Child with chickenpox and fever → paracetamol, never aspirin (Reye's syndrome).
Paracetamol relieves pain and fever but does NOT reduce inflammation. The safe choice for children and people who can't take aspirin.
Lowers fever by acting directly on the hypothalamus.
Used when aspirin causes allergy or stomach upset, and for children with fever.
Overdose destroys liver cells → liver failure and death, especially in heavy drinkers.
Appears safe for short-term use in pregnancy.
Maximum 4,000 mg (4 g) per day.
Paracetamol has no anti-inflammatory effect, unlike aspirin and NSAIDs.
NSAIDs work like aspirin: they block COX enzymes, reducing pain, fever and inflammation.
COX-1 protects the stomach lining. COX-2 drives pain and inflammation.
Non-selective (ibuprofen, diclofenac, indomethacin, naproxen) block both; celecoxib selectively blocks COX-2.
Uses: arthritis, musculoskeletal pain, mild to moderate pain, fever.
Side effects: GI ulcer and bleeding, dizziness, heart failure and BP changes, kidney problems, rash.
Aspirin allergy = contraindication to all NSAIDs.
Avoid in the third trimester and during breastfeeding.
Why do NSAIDs cause ulcers? They block COX-1, which protects the stomach.
Opioids act on the body's own pain receptors (mu, kappa, delta). Morphine is the prototype for moderate to severe pain.
Mu receptor: pain relief, respiratory depression, euphoria, small pupils, constipation.
Pure agonists: morphine, codeine, methadone. Mixed agonist-antagonists: pentazocine, buprenorphine.
Morphine uses: severe pain (labor, MI), breathlessness in pulmonary edema, pre-operative sedation.
Side effects: respiratory depression, constipation, low BP on standing, urine retention, vomiting, raised ICP, small pupils.
Overdose triad: coma, respiratory depression, pinpoint pupils → IV naloxone.
Tolerance develops to pain relief and respiratory depression, but NOT to pinpoint pupils or constipation.
Codeine: weak; turned into morphine in the liver; mild-moderate pain, often with paracetamol.
Fentanyl: very potent, fast, short; epidural for labor; patches can cause fatal hypoventilation.
Unconscious patient, slow breathing, pinpoint pupils → opioid overdose → naloxone.
Naloxone and naltrexone block opioid receptors. Naloxone rescues an overdose; naltrexone helps treat addiction.
Naloxone: IV, IM or SC; drug of choice for opioid overdose.
Naltrexone: oral; with counselling for opioid or alcohol dependence.
Tolerance and dependence develop fast; withdrawal can start after only 3 days of use.
Withdrawal: tremor, sweating, fever, fast breathing, dilated pupils.
Methadone is used to manage opioid dependence.
Opioid overdose antidote → naloxone.
No single anesthetic does everything, so several drugs are combined: balanced anesthesia.
Goals: sedation, unconsciousness and amnesia, muscle relaxation, blocked reflexes, pain relief.
Premedication: benzodiazepine (anxiety), antiemetic, opioid (pain), atropine (secretions, bradycardia), antihistamine, muscle relaxant.
Balanced anesthesia = premedication + IV drug for induction + inhaled drug for maintenance.
Why give atropine before surgery? To prevent bradycardia and reduce secretions.
Inhaled anesthetics maintain anesthesia. Their strength is measured by MAC: the lower the MAC, the more potent.
Nitrous oxide: good pain relief, quick smooth onset and recovery, little effect on heart and breathing; poor muscle relaxant; risk of diffusion hypoxia.
Halothane: pleasant, potent; poor pain relief and muscle relaxation; lowers BP and heart rate; relaxes the uterus (more bleeding after delivery).
Halothane is used for inhalation induction in children.
Halothane + succinylcholine → malignant hyperthermia risk.
Low MAC = high potency. Halothane is more potent than nitrous oxide.
IV anesthetics start anesthesia quickly. Each has a special feature to remember.
Thiopental: unconscious within 25 seconds; poor pain relief; laryngospasm; contraindicated in porphyria.
Propofol: has largely replaced thiopental; low nausea; strong respiratory depressant; pain on injection; for sedating intubated patients.
Ketamine: “dissociative”; strong pain relief, breathing not depressed, raises BP and heart rate. Good for asthmatics and hypovolemic patients; bad in hypertension. Vivid dreams after.
Etomidate: for patients with heart disease or shock; lowers cortisol.
Midazolam: the water-soluble benzodiazepine for IV sedation.
IV anesthetic that raises BP and is good in asthma and shock → ketamine.
Local anesthetics block sodium channels in nerves, stopping pain signals in one area without putting the patient to sleep.
Amides (lidocaine, bupivacaine): metabolized in the liver; more systemic toxicity.
Esters (procaine, tetracaine, benzocaine): broken down in blood; more allergy.
Lidocaine: the most used; works in 3 minutes; also an IV antiarrhythmic.
Types: topical, infiltration, nerve block, spinal.
Side effects: CNS and cardiovascular depression, allergy.
Adding adrenaline slows absorption → longer effect and less toxicity.
Avoid adrenaline-containing LA in heart disease, arrhythmia, thyrotoxicosis, uncontrolled hypertension, or with β-blockers or TCAs.
Avoid accidental IV injection.
Why add adrenaline to lidocaine? It constricts vessels, so the drug stays longer and less reaches the blood.
Most strokes are ischemic (87%). First find out with a CT scan whether it is a clot or a bleed, because treatment is different.
Support breathing and circulation first.
Prevent repeat ischemic stroke: antiplatelets (aspirin, clopidogrel); anticoagulants (warfarin) if atrial fibrillation.
Don't lower BP in acute ischemic stroke unless it is over 220/120 or there is another emergency. If needed: labetalol or nicardipine.
Hemorrhagic stroke: no standard drug; manage BP and intracranial pressure (nimodipine).
tPA and statins play a key role in ischemic stroke.
BP 190/100 in acute ischemic stroke → usually leave it untreated.
Two groups: psychomotor stimulants (excitement, euphoria, less fatigue) and hallucinogens (change thoughts and mood).
Amphetamine, cocaine and methylphenidate can trigger seizures.
Hallucinogens change thinking and mood, with little effect on the brainstem and spinal cord.
The weakest diuretics. Today they are used mostly for the eye (glaucoma) and for mountain sickness, not to remove fluid.
They block carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule, so less NaHCO₃ is reabsorbed and a little more urine is made.
In the eye, the same block means less aqueous humor is made, so eye pressure falls.
Uses: glaucoma (acetazolamide, dorzolamide), mountain sickness, catamenial epilepsy.
Side effects: metabolic acidosis, potassium loss, kidney stones.
Prototype: acetazolamide.
The only diuretic group that acts mainly in the proximal tubule.
A diuretic that causes acidosis (not alkalosis) → carbonic anhydrase inhibitor or K⁺-sparing diuretic.
The strongest diuretics. They remove a lot of water fast, which makes them the drug for emergencies like acute pulmonary edema.
They block the Na⁺/K⁺/2Cl⁻ cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle.
This part reabsorbs 25–30% of filtered salt, and later parts can't make up for it, so the diuresis is the biggest.
More calcium and magnesium are also lost in the urine.
By mouth, the effect starts in about 30 minutes and lasts up to 6 hours.
Uses: acute pulmonary edema, edema from heart, liver or kidney disease, acute renal failure, hypercalcemia.
Side effects: low K⁺, low Mg²⁺, low Na⁺, metabolic alkalosis, dehydration, hypotension.
Also: high uric acid (gout), high blood sugar, and hearing damage (ototoxicity).
Drugs: furosemide, bumetanide, torsemide, ethacrynic acid.
Low K⁺ from loop diuretics increases digoxin toxicity.
NSAIDs reduce their effect. Aminoglycosides add to ear and kidney damage.
Once-daily furosemide is not enough for hypertension; it is given 2–3 times a day.
Hearing loss in a patient on furosemide + gentamicin → two ototoxic drugs together.
Moderate, long-acting diuretics. The everyday diuretic for high blood pressure.
They block the Na⁺/Cl⁻ cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule.
Only about 5% of filtered sodium is handled there, so the effect is moderate.
First weeks: BP falls because blood volume falls. After 6–8 weeks: volume returns to normal, but vessel resistance stays lower.
Uses: hypertension, mild edema, kidney stones from high urine calcium, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
Side effects: low K⁺, low Na⁺, low Mg²⁺, but HIGH calcium.
Also: high blood sugar, high lipids, high uric acid. Thiazides are the diuretics most linked to gout.
Can cause allergy in people allergic to sulfonamides.
Prototype: hydrochlorothiazide. Others: chlorthalidone, indapamide.
Given once daily.
They keep calcium in the body, which helps elderly women with osteoporosis.
In Ethiopia, the usual add-on when amlodipine alone is not enough.
Loop diuretics → calcium goes DOWN. Thiazides → calcium goes UP.
Weak on their own, but they keep potassium in the body. Mostly given together with other diuretics, or when there is too much aldosterone.
They act at the end of the nephron (late distal tubule and collecting duct).
Spironolactone and eplerenone block the aldosterone receptor. Amiloride and triamterene block sodium channels directly.
Less sodium is reabsorbed, so less potassium is pushed out into the urine.
Uses: primary hyperaldosteronism; secondary hyperaldosteronism from heart failure, cirrhosis or nephrotic syndrome.
Also given with thiazides or loop diuretics to prevent potassium loss.
Main danger: hyperkalemia, especially with kidney disease, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, β-blockers or NSAIDs.
Spironolactone can cause gynecomastia and impotence.
They can also cause metabolic acidosis.
Patient on an ACE inhibitor + spironolactone → watch for HIGH potassium.
Mannitol works like a sponge: it holds water inside the kidney tubule. It is used to bring down pressure in the brain and the eye.
Osmotic diuretics are filtered but not reabsorbed, so they keep water in the tubule.
ADH antagonists (e.g. tolvaptan) block the V2 receptor, so the body loses only water.
Mannitol: raised intracranial pressure (acute brain injury), raised eye pressure, acute renal failure.
Tolvaptan: low sodium (hyponatremia).
Mannitol and urea are given IV only. Glycerin and isosorbide work by mouth.
Head injury with raised intracranial pressure → mannitol.

RAAS is the body's long-term blood pressure controller. When BP or salt falls, the kidney releases renin, and the chain ends with angiotensin II and aldosterone, which push BP back up. Many BP drugs cut this chain.
Renin is released when BP falls, blood volume falls, sodium is low, or β1 receptors on the kidney are stimulated.
lines.ref: CVS p.6, RCVS p.32, RCVS p.34

lines.text: Renin → angiotensin I → (ACE) → angiotensin II.
Angiotensin II squeezes vessels, activates the sympathetic system, and releases aldosterone, which keeps sodium and water.
Drugs that block the chain: renin inhibitors, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, aldosterone antagonists. β-blockers also reduce renin release.
Short-term BP control = sympathetic system and baroreflex. Long-term = RAAS.
Why do β-blockers lower renin? β1 receptors on the kidney's JG cells trigger renin release.
ACE inhibitors stop the body from making angiotensin II, so vessels relax and less salt is kept. They also protect the heart and kidneys over the long term.
They block ACE, so less angiotensin II and less aldosterone are made.
They also stop bradykinin from being broken down. Bradykinin widens vessels, but it also causes the dry cough and angioedema.
Uses: hypertension, heart failure, after MI, diabetic kidney disease, chronic kidney disease.
Side effects: low BP after the first dose, dry cough (5–20%), high potassium, loss of taste.
Can cause acute kidney failure in bilateral renal artery stenosis.
Angioedema: rare (0.1–0.5%) but can kill. Swelling of lips, tongue, throat.
Contraindicated: pregnancy, bilateral renal artery stenosis, high potassium, past angioedema.
Captopril: not a prodrug, fast onset, short action (6–12 h).
Enalapril is a prodrug. Its active form, enalaprilat, is given IV in hypertensive emergencies.
Lisinopril is not processed by the liver, so it can be used in liver disease.
No effect on glucose, lipids or uric acid.
The cough goes away about 4 days after stopping. Switching to an ARB usually helps.
Dry cough on an ACE inhibitor → switch to an ARB. Pregnant → never an ACE inhibitor.
ARBs block angiotensin II at its receptor. They give the same benefits as ACE inhibitors, without the bradykinin cough.
They block the AT1 receptor, where angiotensin II does most of its damage.
They work no matter how angiotensin II was made.
They don't affect bradykinin, so cough and angioedema are less common.
Uses: hypertension, heart failure (valsartan, candesartan), diabetic kidney disease (losartan, irbesartan).
In heart failure they are used when the patient can't tolerate an ACE inhibitor.
Side effects: high potassium, low BP. Stop in pregnancy.
All end in “-sartan”. Most are taken once daily.
A patient who coughs on an ACE inhibitor → change to an ARB.
The only drug that blocks renin itself, the very first step of RAAS. It is not better than ACE inhibitors or ARBs.
It blocks renin, so angiotensin I, angiotensin II and aldosterone all fall.
Use: hypertension.
Side effects: diarrhea; rarely angioedema and kidney problems.
Contraindicated in pregnancy, kidney failure, and together with ACE inhibitors or ARBs.
Very low absorption (about 2.5%). Fatty meals reduce it further.
Aliskiren + an ACE inhibitor → contraindicated combination.
Hypertension is blood pressure that stays high. It slowly damages the heart, brain and kidneys. Treating it cuts strokes by 40–50%.
Primary (essential) hypertension: 85–90% of cases, no single cause. Secondary: 10–15%, caused by kidney, thyroid or adrenal disease, pregnancy, etc.
Drivers: an overactive sympathetic system, an overactive RAAS, and damaged vessel lining.
Complications: heart attack, stroke, heart failure, kidney failure.
Treatment lowers stroke by 40–50% and heart attack by 16–30%.
Diagnose only after high readings on two different days.
Risk factors: age, family history, stress, salt, weight, alcohol.
Read the cut-off carefully in each question. Her two files use different definitions (see the flag below).

flags.text: Her two files define hypertension differently. CVS p.4 uses ≥140/90 mmHg. Renal & CVS p.64-65 uses ≥130/80 mmHg (stage 1 = 130–139/80–89, stage 2 = ≥140/90). Ask which one her department and the exit exam use.

lines.text: Every hypertensive patient starts with lifestyle changes, and keeps them even after starting drugs.
Lose weight to a BMI under 25.
Salt under 6 g a day, about one teaspoon. Don't add salt at the table.
Eat a DASH-type diet: fruits, vegetables, low-fat dairy, less fat.
Alcohol: at most 2 drinks a day for men, 1 for women.
Brisk walking 30 minutes a day. Stop smoking. Manage stress.
Hidden salt: bread, processed meat, cheese, packet soups, tomato paste.
Each kilogram lost lowers systolic BP by about 1–2 mmHg.
Lifestyle alone lowers BP by about 5–10 mmHg, enough for some mild cases.
Who needs lifestyle changes? ALL hypertensive patients, not just the mild ones.
These drugs calm the sympathetic nervous system. For nurses the most important one is methyldopa, the safe choice in pregnancy.
Clonidine and methyldopa stimulate α2 receptors in the brainstem, so less sympathetic signal goes out and BP falls.
Methyldopa is turned into α-methyl noradrenaline, which does the work.
Prazosin blocks α1 receptors on blood vessels, so they relax.
Clonidine: mild to moderate hypertension; withdrawal from opioids, alcohol or nicotine.
Clonidine side effects: dry mouth, sedation. Stopping suddenly causes a rebound hypertensive crisis, so taper it over 2–4 days.
Methyldopa: the preferred BP drug in pregnancy. Side effects: sedation, depression, hemolytic anemia, liver damage.
lines.ref: CVS p.41, CVS p.45, RCVS p.77

lines.text: Prazosin: hypertension with an enlarged prostate. The first dose can drop BP when standing, so give it at bedtime.
Methyldopa dose: 250–1000 mg by mouth twice daily, maximum 3 g/day.
These drugs work best together with a diuretic.
A patient missed two clonidine doses and now has a racing heart, sweating and very high BP → rebound hypertension.
They relax blood vessel walls directly. The body fights back with a fast heart rate and water retention, so they are usually combined with a β-blocker and a diuretic.
lines.ref: CVS p.57, CVS p.61, RCVS p.80

lines.text: Hydralazine and minoxidil dilate arteries only. Nitroprusside dilates arteries and veins.
Minoxidil opens K⁺ channels in vessel muscle.
Nitroprusside releases nitric oxide.
Hydralazine: severe hypertension. IV hydralazine is the drug of choice for severe hypertension in pregnancy. Also used with nitrates in heart failure.
Hydralazine side effects: headache, fast heart rate, fluid retention, lupus-like syndrome.
Minoxidil: severe hypertension. Side effects: excess hair growth, edema, fast heart rate. Topical minoxidil treats baldness.
Nitroprusside: hypertensive emergencies, by IV infusion. Works immediately, lasts about 2 minutes.
Nitroprusside turns into cyanide in light, so the bottle is wrapped in dark paper.
Minoxidil must be given with a β-blocker and a loop diuretic.
Why is the nitroprusside infusion covered? Light turns it into cyanide.

flags.text: CVS p.55 calls hydralazine a “K⁺ channel opener”. That is minoxidil's mechanism. Renal & CVS p.78 only says hydralazine acts directly on artery muscle. Check with her teacher which one the exam expects.

lines.text: CCBs stop calcium from entering muscle cells, so vessels relax. There are two families: one works mostly on vessels (amlodipine), the other mostly on the heart (verapamil, diltiazem).
They block L-type calcium channels.
Dihydropyridines (amlodipine, nifedipine) relax vessels and lower BP.
Verapamil and diltiazem act on the heart: slower rate, weaker contraction.
Uses: hypertension, all types of angina, and (verapamil, diltiazem) atrial fibrillation and other fast atrial rhythms.
Amlodipine/nifedipine side effects: headache, flushing, ankle swelling, low BP.
Verapamil side effects: constipation, AV block.
Amlodipine is the first-line drug for uncomplicated hypertension in Ethiopia.
Avoid verapamil and diltiazem with β-blockers, in heart failure, and when systolic BP is under 90.
Ankle swelling → amlodipine/nifedipine. Constipation → verapamil.
Four classes are first line: ACE inhibitors/ARBs, CCBs and thiazides, with β-blockers for special cases. In Ethiopia, treatment usually starts with amlodipine.
First line with no other disease: ACE inhibitor, ARB, CCB or thiazide.
Ethiopian order: start amlodipine → add a thiazide → third, an ACE inhibitor.
β-blockers are preferred for young patients, and for patients with a fast heart rate or angina.
Black patients respond better to diuretics and CCBs than to β-blockers and ACE inhibitors.
ACE inhibitors protect the kidneys, especially in diabetics.
One drug is best for compliance and cost, but many patients need two or more.
Low doses of several drugs give fewer side effects than a high dose of one.
Why amlodipine first in Ethiopia? It works in all races, needs less lab monitoring, and is safe for women who may become pregnant.
In pregnancy, some BP drugs harm the baby. Know the safe list and the forbidden list.
Safe: methyldopa; β-blockers in the third trimester; modified-release nifedipine.
Hypertensive crisis: IV labetalol or IV hydralazine.
Preventing seizures in pre-eclampsia and eclampsia: magnesium sulfate is the drug of choice.
Forbidden: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, aliskiren and thiazides, also for women who could become pregnant without contraception.
ACE inhibitors harm the fetus: low BP, no urine, kidney failure, malformation or death.
A pregnant woman is on lisinopril → stop it and switch to methyldopa or nifedipine.
In heart failure the pump can't keep up with the body's needs. The body's emergency responses help at first, but later make things worse, so most heart failure drugs block those responses.
Low cardiac output triggers the sympathetic system (fast heart rate), RAAS (salt and water kept), ADH and vessel squeezing.
Over time the heart thickens and changes shape (remodeling), and output falls further.
Systolic failure = weak squeeze. Diastolic failure = stiff heart that fills poorly.
Signs: fast heart rate, tiredness with exercise, shortness of breath, swelling of legs and lungs, enlarged heart.
Causes: ischemic heart disease and MI, hypertension, valve disease, cardiomyopathy, congenital disease.
Too much preload → diuretics, salt restriction, venodilators.
Too much afterload → arteriolar vasodilators.
Weak contraction → inotropes. Fast heart rate → β-blockers.
The main direct result of low cardiac output: tiredness and poor exercise tolerance.
The failing heart is a tired pump. Digoxin makes each beat stronger and slows the rhythm, so the heart fills better between beats.
It blocks the Na⁺/K⁺ pump in heart cells.
Sodium builds up inside, so less calcium is pushed out.
More calcium inside → stronger contraction.
It also acts on the vagus nerve → slower heart rate.
Uses: heart failure and atrial fibrillation.
The toxic dose is close to the normal dose (narrow therapeutic index), so blood levels are monitored.
Low potassium makes a normal dose toxic. High calcium does too.
Most diuretics lower potassium, so watch patients on digoxin + a diuretic closely.
Toxicity: nausea, vomiting, visual changes, arrhythmias, gynecomastia, vertigo.
Treatment: stop digoxin and diuretics, correct potassium, atropine for slow heart rate, lidocaine for arrhythmias.
Antidote: digoxin immune Fab (Digibind).
Quinidine and verapamil raise digoxin levels.
Dose: 0.125–0.5 mg by mouth daily.
Nausea + blurred vision in a patient on digoxin and furosemide → low potassium has caused digoxin toxicity.
Short-term IV boosters for the heart, used in hospital for acute severe heart failure.
They stimulate β1 receptors. More calcium enters heart cells, so contraction is stronger.
Given only by IV infusion, for a short time, in acute heart failure.
Dobutamine is the most used inotrope after digoxin. Tolerance can develop after about 72 hours.
Dopamine: only low to moderate doses. High doses squeeze blood vessels.
Dobutamine's half-life is only 2.4 minutes, which is why it runs as a continuous infusion.
Dobutamine by mouth? No. It is IV only, for short-term use.
For long-term heart failure, diuretics relieve the fluid, and ACE inhibitors and β-blockers help patients live longer.
lines.ref: CVS p.103, CVS p.105, RCVS p.113

lines.text: Diuretics, especially loop diuretics, are the mainstay. They reduce fluid and swelling but don't make the heart stronger.
ACE inhibitors reduce the heart's workload, improve symptoms and reduce deaths. First line with diuretics.
ARBs are used if an ACE inhibitor isn't tolerated. In heart failure they are not as effective as ACE inhibitors.
β-blockers (carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, bisoprolol) reduce hospital stays and deaths.
If ACE inhibitors or β-blockers aren't tolerated: hydralazine + isosorbide dinitrate. It especially helps Black patients.
Before starting an ACE inhibitor, lower the diuretic dose to avoid low BP.
Spironolactone is added when there is marked secondary hyperaldosteronism.
β-blockers can worsen acute heart failure, but they help chronic heart failure.
Angina is chest pain when heart muscle gets less oxygen than it needs. It is a symptom, not a disease.
Demand rises with heart rate, force of contraction and wall tension. Supply depends on coronary blood flow.
Drugs either lower demand or increase supply.
Pain: pressing, behind the sternum, spreading to the left arm, shoulder or face.
Stable angina: predictable, with exercise, cold, eating or emotion; caused by atherosclerosis; settles with rest.
Variant (Prinzmetal) angina: coronary spasm, comes at rest. Treat with nitrates and CCBs.
Unstable angina: more frequent, with less effort or at rest; small clots on a cracked plaque. It is an acute coronary syndrome and needs hospital care.
Unstable angina in hospital: sublingual nitroglycerin, aspirin, an anticoagulant, and oxygen if saturation is low.
Chest pain at rest with normal exercise tolerance → variant angina → CCB, not a β-blocker.
Nitroglycerin under the tongue relieves angina within minutes, mainly by widening veins so the heart has less blood to pump.
Nitrates are turned into nitric oxide, which relaxes smooth muscle.
Veins widen most → less blood returns to the heart (lower preload).
Arteries and coronary arteries also widen → lower afterload and more oxygen to the heart.
Used for all types of angina.
Sublingual for an acute attack: works in 2–3 minutes, lasts about 2 hours.
Long-acting tablets or patches for prevention.
Side effects: throbbing headache, flushing, dizziness on standing, fast heart rate.
Swallowed nitrates are mostly destroyed by the liver (first pass), which is why they go under the tongue.
Tolerance develops quickly, so long-acting forms need a nitrate-free period each day.
Never with sildenafil: dangerous drop in BP.
Patch dose: 0.2–0.4 mg per hour.
A patient on nitrates asks about sildenafil → contraindicated, severe hypotension.
Both lower the heart's oxygen demand. β-blockers are best for angina on exertion. CCBs are best for spasm (variant angina).
β-blockers lower heart rate, force and BP, so the heart needs less oxygen.
CCBs relax coronary arteries and lower afterload. Verapamil and diltiazem also slow the heart.
β-blockers: stable and unstable angina; they reduce deaths after MI. Not useful in variant angina.
CCBs: the most effective prevention for variant angina; also used in stable angina.
Avoid verapamil and diltiazem with a weak ventricle, AV block, or systolic BP under 90.
β-blocker side effects: slow heart rate, AV block, heart failure, and hidden signs of low blood sugar.
Never stop a β-blocker suddenly; it can trigger an MI.
Non-selective β-blockers are avoided in asthma and COPD.
A diabetic on propranolol doesn't feel the warning signs of hypoglycemia, because the β-blocker hides them.
Clots on cracked plaques cause unstable angina and heart attacks. Low-dose aspirin stops platelets from clumping together.
Aspirin blocks thromboxane production in platelets.
Clopidogrel blocks the platelet ADP receptor.
Aspirin 80–325 mg daily for stable and unstable angina.
In acute MI, aspirin reduces deaths by 23%. In unstable angina, it halves MI and death.
Higher doses increase bleeding.
Clopidogrel: 300 mg loading dose, then 75 mg daily. Combined with aspirin in unstable angina.
Statins are also standard in unstable angina, for example high-dose atorvastatin 80 mg/day.
Low-dose aspirin is for preventing clots. The main thing to watch is bleeding.
A normal heartbeat starts in the SA node and follows a fixed path. An arrhythmia means the wrong rate, the wrong starting point, or the wrong path.
Normal: rate 60–100; SA node → atria → AV node → bundle of His and Purkinje fibers → ventricles.
Abnormal impulse formation: a pacemaker fires too fast or too slow, or extra beats are triggered.
Abnormal conduction: a block (e.g. AV block) or re-entry, where the signal loops around.
Fast rhythms by rate: simple tachycardia 100–150, paroxysmal 150–250, flutter 250–350, fibrillation over 350.
Causes: low potassium, ischemia, injury, drugs such as digoxin.
Drug classes: I = Na⁺ channel blockers, II = β-blockers, III = K⁺ channel blockers, IV = Ca²⁺ channel blockers. Others: adenosine, magnesium, digoxin.
Low potassium can cause arrhythmias on its own, and it also makes digoxin toxic.
They block sodium channels so heart cells fire less easily. The one nurses meet most is lidocaine, given IV after an MI.
Class IA (quinidine, procainamide): side effects include cinchonism (tinnitus, GI upset, vision problems) and torsades.
Procainamide can cause a lupus-like syndrome, more often in slow acetylators.
Class IB (lidocaine): after MI, heart surgery, and digoxin-toxicity arrhythmias. The least cardiotoxic, but can cause seizures.
Class IC (flecainide): limited use, because it can cause sudden death after MI.
Lidocaine is given IV because swallowed lidocaine is destroyed by the liver.
Quinidine raises digoxin levels and increases its toxicity.
Why is lidocaine never given by mouth for arrhythmias? First-pass metabolism in the liver.
Class II = β-blockers, III = potassium channel blockers like amiodarone, IV = calcium channel blockers like verapamil. Amiodarone works for almost any arrhythmia but has many side effects.
Class II, β-blockers: slow the SA and AV nodes. Used after MI and for fast atrial rhythms. IV esmolol for acute episodes.
Class III, amiodarone: any arrhythmia. Half-life over 80 days.
Amiodarone side effects: lung fibrosis, thyroid problems, blue-gray skin, sun sensitivity, corneal deposits, liver damage.
Sotalol: life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias.
Class IV, verapamil and diltiazem: fast atrial rhythms. Side effects: constipation, AV block.
Verapamil + a β-blocker or digoxin → risk of AV block. Verapamil also raises digoxin levels.
A patient on amiodarone develops a cough and breathlessness → think lung fibrosis. Also check the thyroid.
Adenosine is the IV drug of choice to stop paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia, and it works in seconds. Magnesium treats torsades de pointes.
Adenosine is given IV. Its half-life is under 10 seconds.
Side effects: flushing, shortness of breath, sedation.
Magnesium sulfate: torsades de pointes.
Theophylline blocks adenosine's effect.
Drugs that can cause torsades: class IA and class III antiarrhythmics, thioridazine, tricyclic antidepressants.
Drug of choice for paroxysmal SVT → adenosine.
Statins lower “bad” LDL cholesterol by slowing the liver's cholesterol factory. They are the most effective lipid drugs.
They block HMG-CoA reductase, the key enzyme for making cholesterol.
The liver makes more LDL receptors and pulls LDL out of the blood.
LDL can fall by up to 60% (rosuvastatin).
First-line treatment for high LDL; standard after MI and in unstable angina.
Side effects: muscle pain, myopathy, rhabdomyolysis (check CK); liver damage (check liver tests).
Not used in pregnancy or breastfeeding.
Names end in “-statin”: atorvastatin, simvastatin, rosuvastatin.
Gemfibrozil increases the risk of rhabdomyolysis.
A patient on a statin has muscle pain and dark urine → think rhabdomyolysis and check CK.
These are mainly for patients who can't take statins, or whose main problem is high triglycerides.
Fibrates (gemfibrozil, fenofibrate): lower triglycerides. Side effects: gallstones, muscle inflammation.
Bile acid sequestrants (cholestyramine): bind bile in the gut. Side effects: GI upset, poor absorption of fat-soluble vitamins. Avoid if triglycerides are high.
Niacin: lowers VLDL and LDL, raises HDL. Side effects: flushing (aspirin helps), liver damage, high blood sugar.
Ezetimibe: blocks cholesterol absorption in the gut.
Omega-3 fatty acids: severe high triglycerides, 3–4 g/day with food. Can prolong bleeding.
Bile acid sequestrants block absorption of other oral drugs such as warfarin, thiazides and digoxin.
Flushing on niacin → aspirin taken beforehand reduces it.

An ulcer forms when the stomach's attackers (acid, pepsin, H. pylori, NSAIDs) win over its defenders (mucus, bicarbonate, blood flow, prostaglandins). Treatment either weakens the attack or strengthens the defense.
Parietal cells make acid when three signals arrive: acetylcholine (vagus nerve), gastrin (from food), and histamine.
The final step is the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump (proton pump), which pushes acid into the stomach.
GERD = stomach acid flowing back up into the esophagus.
Main causes of PUD: H. pylori, NSAIDs, stress.
GERD symptoms: burning in the chest or throat; severe cases cause difficulty swallowing and chest pain.
Non-drug advice: stop smoking; avoid alcohol, caffeine and cola drinks.
Drug groups: antacids, H2 blockers, PPIs, misoprostol, mucosal protectives, and antibiotics for H. pylori.
Long-term GERD can cause Barrett's esophagus (~10%), which is linked to esophageal cancer.
Three things switch on acid: acetylcholine, gastrin, histamine. One pump makes it: H⁺/K⁺-ATPase.
Antacids are weak bases that neutralize acid already in the stomach. They give fast relief but don't stop acid being made.
They react with HCl to form less acidic, poorly absorbed salts, raising stomach pH.
Above pH 4, pepsin stops working, which also protects the lining.
Examples: aluminium hydroxide, magnesium hydroxide, magnesium trisilicate.
Most products combine aluminium and magnesium compounds.
Antacids neutralize acid that is already there. H2 blockers and PPIs reduce how much is made.
H2 blockers stop histamine from switching on acid production. They work best at night, when acid depends mostly on histamine.
They block histamine at H2 receptors on parietal cells, reducing 24-hour acid by 60–70%.
Uses: peptic ulcer, GERD, Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (a tumor that makes gastrin and drives acid very high).
Drugs: cimetidine, ranitidine, nizatidine, famotidine.
Strong on night-time acid; weaker on acid after meals, which is also driven by gastrin and acetylcholine.
Which drug class is especially good at night-time acid? H2 blockers.
PPIs switch off the final acid pump itself, so they are the strongest acid reducers.
They irreversibly block the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase (proton pump) in parietal cells, stopping 90–98% of daily acid, both fasting and after meals.
Uses: peptic ulcer, GERD, Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.
Part of every H. pylori eradication regimen.
Prevention and treatment of NSAID-induced ulcers.
Drugs end in “-prazole”: omeprazole, esomeprazole, lansoprazole, pantoprazole, rabeprazole.
H2 blockers: 60–70% acid reduction. PPIs: 90–98%. PPIs are stronger.
These drugs strengthen the stomach's defenses instead of attacking acid.
Misoprostol (a prostaglandin E1 copy): more mucus and bicarbonate, better blood flow, a little less acid.
Misoprostol is contraindicated in pregnancy: it can cause abortion, premature birth or birth defects.
Misoprostol side effects: diarrhea (10–40%) and nausea.
Sucralfate: forms a sticky coat over the ulcer in acid.
Bismuth: kills bacteria, blocks pepsin, increases mucus, and coats the ulcer.
A pregnant woman with an ulcer → never misoprostol.
If H. pylori causes the ulcer, the bacteria must be killed or the ulcer comes back. Treatment always combines acid suppression with antibiotics.
Triple therapy: PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin for 14 days, 80–85% effective. Use metronidazole instead of amoxicillin in penicillin allergy.
Quadruple therapy: bismuth + metronidazole + tetracycline + a PPI or H2 blocker.
Triple therapy doses: clarithromycin 500 mg + amoxicillin 1 g, twice daily, with a PPI.
Penicillin allergy in triple therapy → swap amoxicillin for metronidazole.
