flags.text: The GI slide says quadruple therapy is a 7-day course. The speaker notes on the same slide say 14 days. Check which duration her teacher uses.

lines.text: Diarrhea = the gut moves too fast and absorbs too little fluid. Antidiarrheals slow the gut down, soak up toxins, or reduce fluid secretion.
Loperamide and diphenoxylate act on opioid receptors in the gut wall, reduce acetylcholine release, and slow peristalsis.
Antimotility: loperamide, diphenoxylate. The most effective group.
Adsorbents: aluminium hydroxide, methylcellulose. Much weaker, and they block absorption of other drugs.
Bismuth subsalicylate: reduces fluid secretion; used for traveler's diarrhea.
Bismuth turns the tongue and stools black. This is harmless.
A patient on bismuth reports black stools → expected side effect.
Laxatives speed up stool or soften it. Each group does it a different way.
Stimulants: senna, bisacodyl, castor oil.
Bulk laxatives: methylcellulose, psyllium, bran.
Osmotic/saline: magnesium citrate, magnesium hydroxide.
Stool softeners: docusate. Lubricants: mineral oil, glycerin suppositories.
Laxative = soft formed stool. Cathartic = stronger action, liquid stool.
Laxatives can reduce the effect of slow-release oral drugs by rushing them through the gut.
Docusate works by mixing water and fat into the stool, making it softer.
TB bacteria grow slowly, hide inside cells, have a thick wall, and become resistant to a single drug quickly. So treatment always uses several drugs for many months.
M. tuberculosis spreads by droplets from coughing or sneezing. M. bovis spreads through milk from infected cows.
First-line drugs: isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, streptomycin. Most effective, acceptable toxicity.
Second-line drugs are more toxic and less effective; used only for resistant TB.
Treatment success depends on compliance, toxicity, drug interactions and other diseases.
Why never treat TB with a single drug? Resistance develops quickly.
The most active and safest TB drug. It blocks the bacteria from building their special cell wall.
The bacteria's own enzyme (KatG) activates isoniazid.
Active isoniazid blocks mycolic acid synthesis, which the TB cell wall needs.
It kills dividing bacteria and stops resting ones; it also reaches bacteria inside cells.
Used in all TB treatment and prevention regimens.
Alone for latent TB, and as TB prevention in people with HIV.
Side effects: hepatitis (more in alcoholics and pregnancy), peripheral neuropathy, CNS effects (memory loss, psychosis, seizures), lupus-like reaction.
Neuropathy comes from pyridoxine (B6) deficiency; giving pyridoxine prevents it.
Slow acetylators get neuropathy more easily.
Burning or numb feet on TB treatment → isoniazid neuropathy → give vitamin B6.
A powerful TB killer that also speeds up the liver's breakdown of many other drugs, which causes many interactions.
It blocks bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase, so the bacteria can't make RNA.
First-line for all forms of TB; alternative to INH for latent TB; part of leprosy treatment; MRSA.
Kills bacteria both inside and outside cells.
Side effects: rash, low platelets, nephritis, jaundice, hepatitis.
Turns urine, sweat and tears orange. Warn the patient; it is harmless.
Strong enzyme inducer: lowers levels of oral contraceptives, anticoagulants, some anticonvulsants, methadone and HIV protease inhibitors.
Food reduces its absorption.
A woman on rifampin and the pill → contraceptive failure risk; she needs another method.
A TB-only drug whose key danger is the eyes.
Blocks arabinosyl transferase, an enzyme needed to build the mycobacterial cell wall.
Often the fourth drug with INH, rifampin and pyrazinamide.
Most serious side effects: loss of visual acuity and red-green color blindness.
Avoided in children too young to have their vision tested.
About half is excreted unchanged in urine, so adjust the dose in kidney disease.
Blurred vision or trouble telling red from green on TB drugs → ethambutol.
The first drug that reduced TB deaths. It is an injectable aminoglycoside that acts only outside cells.
Blocks protein synthesis on the bacterial ribosome.
A fourth drug when drug resistance is likely.
Used when an injectable drug is needed, e.g. severe or life-threatening TB.
About 80% of strains resistant to INH and rifampin are also resistant to streptomycin.
Streptomycin is an aminoglycoside, so expect the class toxicities: ear and kidney.
Pyrazinamide kills the last hidden bacteria inside acidic cells, which is why TB treatment can be shortened to 6 months.
It is a prodrug, activated by the bacteria's enzyme to pyrazinoic acid.
Works only in acid (pH 5.5), such as inside macrophages.
A front-line drug with INH and rifampin in 6-month regimens, as a “sterilizing” agent.
Side effects: liver toxicity (1–5%), nausea, vomiting, fever, and high uric acid that can cause gout.
Joint pain and high uric acid on TB treatment → pyrazinamide.
Used only when TB resists first-line drugs. They are weaker and more toxic.
Fluoroquinolones (moxifloxacin, gatifloxacin): key drugs for MDR-TB, always combined.
Ethionamide: related to INH. Side effects: GI upset, metallic taste, neuropathy; pyridoxine helps.
PAS (aminosalicylic acid): folate blocker. Causes GI upset, poorly tolerated with peptic ulcer.
Cycloserine: CNS effects including psychosis and suicide risk. Avoid in epilepsy.
Amikacin, kanamycin, capreomycin: injectables for resistant TB; ear and kidney toxicity.
A TB patient with a history of epilepsy → avoid cycloserine.
Leprosy is treated with three drugs together: dapsone, clofazimine and rifampin, for 6–24 months (WHO).
Dapsone blocks folate synthesis, like sulfonamides.
Clofazimine binds bacterial DNA and stops it from copying.
Dapsone side effects: hemolysis, methemoglobinemia, neuropathy, and erythema nodosum leprosum.
Erythema nodosum leprosum is treated with corticosteroids or thalidomide.
Dapsone is also used for Pneumocystis pneumonia in HIV.
Leprosy spreads through broken skin or the respiratory tract.
WHO triple therapy for leprosy: dapsone + clofazimine + rifampin.
Pregnancy needs ovulation, fertilization and implantation. Every contraceptive blocks at least one of these steps.
Stop ovulation: hormones (pills, patch, injection, implant, ring, hormonal IUD).
Stop implantation: copper IUD.
Stop fertilization: spermicides (gels, foams) and barriers (condoms, caps, diaphragms).
Three types of oral pills: combined (estrogen + progestin), mini pills (progestin only), and morning-after pills.
Copper IUD works mainly by preventing implantation, not ovulation.
Combined pills contain estrogen + progestin and mainly stop ovulation. They are up to 99.9% effective when taken correctly.
They suppress FSH and LH, so no egg is released.
They also thin the uterine lining (no implantation) and thicken cervical mucus (no sperm passage).
Monthly pills: 21 days (day 5 to day 26), then 7 pill-free days. 28-pill packs have 7 sugar pills to keep the habit.
Seasonal pills: 84 days on, 7 off, so only 4 periods a year. More spotting early on.
Estrogen side effects: nausea, breast tenderness, headache, skin pigmentation, high blood sugar, thromboembolism, hypertension, gallbladder disease.
Progestin side effects: fatigue, low mood, irregular bleeding, weight gain, hirsutism, ectopic pregnancy.
Contraindicated: thromboembolism, heart failure/edema, undiagnosed vaginal bleeding, pregnancy, breast cancer, liver disease, migraine, hypertension, diabetes, breastfeeding.
Women who are obese, smoke, or are over 35 are better on mini pills.
Failure risk: rifampin, phenytoin, phenobarbitone (enzyme inducers), and some antibiotics.
COCs raise the levels of warfarin, cyclosporine and theophylline.
Thromboembolism on the pill → estrogen. Migraine patient → avoid combined pills.
Progestin-only pills are for women who can't take estrogen. They work mainly by thickening cervical mucus so sperm can't pass.
Used when estrogen is contraindicated: breastfeeding, smokers, women over 35, hypertension, heart, liver or cancer problems, fibroids.
Taken every day at the same time, all year, with no break.
Slightly higher failure rate than combined pills.
Side effects are the progestin ones only: irregular bleeding, weight gain, low mood, ectopic pregnancy.
A 37-year-old obese smoker or a breastfeeding mother wants the pill → mini pill.
Emergency contraception is used after unprotected sex. The sooner it is taken, the better it works.
Indications: failed withdrawal, torn condom, missed pills, detached patch, rape.
Estrogen + levonorgestrel: 2 tablets, twice, 12 hours apart, best within 12 h, up to 72 h; about 75% effective.
Mifepristone ± misoprostol: a single dose, up to 120 hours; 85–100% effective.
Mifepristone blocks progesterone. It can cause heavy uterine bleeding, so it must be used under medical supervision.
The emergency option that works up to 120 hours → mifepristone.
Non-pill hormone methods mean she doesn't have to remember a daily pill.
Patch: both hormones; a new patch weekly for 3 weeks, 1 week off; 99%.
Injection: depot medroxyprogesterone, 150 mg IM every 3 months; 99.7%.
Implant: levonorgestrel rods, every 3–5 years; 98–99%.
Vaginal ring: 3 weeks in, 1 week out.
Levonorgestrel IUD: up to 5 years; 97%.
Contraceptive injection given every 3 months → depot medroxyprogesterone.

notes.title: How drugs work on the skin

lines.text: Drugs put on the skin treat the problem where it is, with fewer side effects in the rest of the body.
Thin skin (scrotum, face, armpit, scalp) absorbs much more than the forearm, so less drug is needed there.
A higher concentration pushes more drug in.
Skin stores the drug, so once-daily application is often enough.
Covering with plastic wrap (occlusion) strongly increases the effect.
Same steroid cream on the face vs the forearm → the face absorbs much more.
Acne starts when hormones make too much oil, pores block, and P. acnes bacteria grow inside. Treatment cuts oil or controls the bacteria.
Benzoyl peroxide: first line for mild to moderate acne without inflammation; kills bacteria, opens pores.
Retinoids (tretinoin, adapalene): clear blocked pores and reduce inflammation.
Oral isotretinoin: only for severe cystic acne. Side effects include dryness, sun sensitivity, and risk of suicide.
Antibiotics for inflamed acne: topical clindamycin (preferred) or erythromycin; oral doxycycline or minocycline.
Salicylic acid and azelaic acid: for mild acne.
All retinoids are contraindicated in pregnancy.
Pregnant woman with acne → no retinoids.
Psoriasis = skin cells multiply too fast, forming red scaly plaques. Treatment slows the cells or calms the immune system.
Mild to moderate: topical retinoids (tazarotene), vitamin D analogues, keratolytics, corticosteroids.
Severe: phototherapy, methotrexate, cyclosporine, or biologics.
Vitamin D analogues (calcipotriene): slow skin cell growth; may raise calcium a little.
Coal tar and salicylic acid: good for scalp psoriasis; help steroids penetrate.
Acitretin (oral): no alcohol, because alcohol converts it to a longer-lasting form.
A patient on acitretin asks about drinking → alcohol is contraindicated.
Hydroquinone lightens dark patches; methoxsalen brings color back in vitiligo; minoxidil and finasteride treat male-pattern baldness.
Hydroquinone: blocks tyrosinase, which makes melanin. Used for freckles and melasma, usually 4%.
Methoxsalen: a psoralen activated by UV light (PUVA) to repigment vitiligo. Use with caution: skin aging and possible cancer.
Minoxidil and finasteride: male-pattern baldness. Finasteride lowers DHT.
Vitiligo → methoxsalen + UVA (PUVA).
Skin infections by staph and strep (impetigo, folliculitis) can be treated with creams and ointments.
Bacitracin: gram-positive bacteria; prevents infection after burns and scrapes. Toxic if given systemically.
Mupirocin: impetigo and gram-positive infections including MRSA.
Polymyxin B: gram-negative bacteria.
“Triple antibiotic” = polymyxin + neomycin + bacitracin, for minor skin wounds.
Impetigo, including MRSA → mupirocin.
